interactive.title: The turning coil
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens, most on one picture, the turning coil. On the left, a north pole and a south pole face each other, with the field drawn as straight lines running across from north to south. Between them sits a rectangular coil of wire seen end-on, so it looks like a line with a dot at each end, its two long sides, turning about its centre. Its angle θ is measured from face-on, square to the field lines. A shaded band shows the field lines passing through the coil, the flux, which is how much of the coil's face the field lines meet: widest face-on, gone edge-on, and back from the other side past edge-on. On the right, two traces run against time: the flux through the coil, as a share of its face-on amount from 1 to −1, and below it the emf, in volts. A marker rides the flux trace showing its slope, and the emf is drawn as how fast the flux falls, that slope turned upside down (Faraday's minus sign; which way round counts as positive is a choice). Arrows on the coil's two sides show which way the emf pushes round the coil, and a lamp joined across the coil's ends shows which way current runs through it. The rule: the emf is set by how fast the flux through the coil is changing. With θ from face-on, the flux share is cos θ, and the emf is its peak × sin θ, so it is zero face-on, at its peak edge-on (90°), zero again face-on from the other side (180°) and at its peak the other way at 270°. Textbooks give the peak as N × B × A × ω: N the turns of wire on the coil, B the field strength in teslas, A the coil's area in square metres and ω = 2π × turns a second, the angular speed from From circle to wave. The coil is drawn as 10 cm by 10 cm, an area of 0.01 m², an example size. On screens that show an idea, the coil can be dragged round by its edge (it wears a ring) or set spinning with a play button, and sliders set its turns a second (0.5 to 5, opening at 2 on the speed screen), its turns of wire (10 to 200, opening at 100) and the field (0.1 to 1.0 T, opening at 0.5 T). Readouts give the emf now, the peak emf and the period. At the opening settings the peak is 100 × 0.5 × 0.01 × 2π × 1 = 3.14 V and the period 1 s. Screen 1 lets you drag the coil and watch the flux band and the flux trace. Screen 2 sets the coil edge-on and asks how much flux passes through it: none, the most, or half. Screen 3 sets it spinning and draws the emf trace under the flux trace: the emf is zero where the flux trace is at its top or bottom and peaks where the flux trace crosses zero, steepest. Screen 4 asks where in the turn the emf is biggest: edge-on, face-on, or halfway between. Screen 5 shows why the emf is a sine: the coil's angle is From circle to wave's arm, measured from the upright (face-on), so the arm's height is the flux share, cos θ, and the up-and-down part of the tip's speed, the part across the field lines, is its speed × sin θ. Shrinking the flux one way and building it the other way are one change, so the arrows on the coil's sides keep their direction from face-on to face-on and flip as the coil passes face-on, each half turn, and the lamp's current reverses with them. Screen 6 asks what reverses each half turn: the direction of the push and of the current; the field between the poles; or nothing, the current just stops for half of each turn. Screen 7 frees the speed slider: at 2 turns a second the peak is 6.28 V and the period 0.5 s, the wave taller and shorter in time together; the emf axis's top tick shows its new scale. Screen 8 asks what doubling the speed does: doubles the peak and halves the period; halves the period only; or doubles the peak only. Screen 9 frees the turns and field sliders: each scales the peak and leaves the period alone. Screen 10 asks about a coil giving 12 V peak, rewound with three times the turns at the same field and speed: 36 V with the same period; 36 V with a third of the period; or 4 V. Screens 11 and 12 are mixed. Screen 11: a coil peaking at 20 V is 30° past face-on; is its emf 10 V (20 × sin 30°), 17.3 V (20 × cos 30°, the flux's shape read instead) or 0 V? Screen 12: this simple coil gives 100 V peak at 50 turns a second, a 50 Hz wave. To make 60 Hz with the same coil and field it turns 60 times a second; is the peak 120 V (100 × 60 ÷ 50), 100 V (speed changing the frequency only) or 83.3 V (the ratio upside down)? Its Why? adds that 60 Hz is the most common frequency on board ship, and that a real generator adjusts its field to hold its voltage, which Three-phase power systems at sea takes up. Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, Why? explains in words, and a right Check draws the answer on the picture. The closing line says where the course goes next: Rms, what the 230 V on a label means for a wave that never stands still.
interactive.ignores: The coil makes far fewer waves a second than a real 50 Hz generator, which makes 50, so you can watch it. The field is drawn perfectly even between flat poles. The picture does not show how the turning coil's ends are joined to the lamp. Nothing loads the coil, so it turns freely. The rest of this note is the writer's reading, not from this lesson's sources: a real generator gets harder to turn as it supplies current; large ones usually keep their coils still and turn the magnet, and have many coils, often with more than one pair of poles, so they make more than one wave a turn, the flux through each coil changing in the same way; and their waves are close to a sine, not exactly one. Puzzle voltages are example figures.

explain.text:
Turn a coil of wire steadily between two magnet poles and the field passing through it grows, shrinks to nothing and builds the other way, over and over. The coil makes a voltage only while that field is changing, and the faster it changes the bigger the voltage, so the voltage is biggest when the coil is edge-on to the field, with none passing through it, and zero when the coil faces the field.

Picture the field as straight lines running across from the north pole to the south. How many of them pass through the coil depends on which way it faces: face-on it catches the most, edge-on they all slip past, and turned on past edge-on they pass through from the other side. That amount of field through the coil is its [[flux]]. A changing flux through a coil makes a push round it, and the push is set by how fast the flux changes, not by how much there is.[^2] A push made this way is called an [[emf]], measured in volts like any voltage. Face-on, the flux is at its most, and for that instant it is neither growing nor shrinking, like a ball at the top of its throw, so the emf is zero. Edge-on, the flux is zero but changing fastest, so the emf is at its peak.

The emf traces a sine wave, and From circle to wave shows why. Measure the coil's angle θ from face-on, which the picture draws as the upright, so the ringed wire is an arm whose height is cos θ: the flux, how much of the coil's face the field lines meet. The arm's tip moves at a steady speed at right angles to the arm, and only its up-and-down part crosses the field lines and changes the flux, that speed × sin θ: nothing when the arm points straight up, face-on, all of it when the arm lies flat, edge-on. The flux's slope is −sin θ, as the slope of cos θ always is, and the emf is drawn as how fast the flux falls, minus its slope, which is Faraday's minus sign; which way round the coil counts as positive is a choice. So the emf is its peak × sin θ: a coil turned steadily in an even field makes an emf that varies as a sine in time.[^3] From face-on to edge-on the flux shrinks, and from edge-on to the next face-on it builds through the coil from the other side. Those are one change, a fall from most one way to most the other way, so the emf keeps its direction for the whole half turn. At face-on the change turns round, so the emf reverses, and the current it drives through a lamp reverses too. That is what alternates: the direction of the push and of the current, not the magnet's field, which stays put. The charge in the wires moves one way and then back, making no journey round the circuit, and current driven like this is [[alternating current]]. For a coil between one pair of poles, one turn draws one whole wave, so its turns a second are the frequency: 50 for UK mains, and 60, the most common frequency on board ship, because it lets motors and generators run faster and so be smaller for a given power.[^1]

A faster turn changes the flux faster, so it gives a bigger emf.[^4] Textbooks add that the peak is N × B × A × ω: the turns of wire N, the field strength B in teslas, the coil's area A in square metres and the angular speed ω. More turns each add their own push, and a stronger field or a bigger coil gives more flux to change. Take the picture's coil, 100 turns, 0.5 T and 0.01 m², turning once a second, so ω = 2π × 1 = 6.28 rad/s: its peak is 100 × 0.5 × 0.01 × 6.28 = 3.14 V, and 30° past face-on its emf is 3.14 × sin 30° = 1.57 V. Turn it twice a second and the peak doubles to 6.28 V while each wave takes half as long, 0.5 s. Of the four, only the speed changes the period too, so in a simple generator turning faster raises the voltage and the frequency together; a real generator holds its voltage by adjusting its field current.[^5] The course's motor puzzle, a motor drawing 10 A while the wattmeter reads 1.6 kW, runs on this wave: the supply's voltage and the motor's current both reverse every half cycle, and the rest of the course is about what happens when they do not reverse together. One coil in an even field is a simplified model. In the writer's reading, not from this lesson's sources, real generators have many coils, often more than one pair of poles, so they make more than one wave a turn, and their waves are close to a sine rather than exactly one. **A coil turned steadily in a magnetic field makes a sine-wave emf,[^3] because its emf follows how fast the flux through it is changing,[^2] so the emf peaks edge-on, where the flux is zero, and reverses as the coil passes face-on, every half turn.**

analogy.text: A harbour basin fills and empties through its entrance as the tide rises and falls. The water level is the flux, and the stream through the entrance is the emf. The stream runs hardest at half tide, when the level is changing fastest, and goes slack at high and low water, when the level is at its highest or lowest and for a moment not changing. Then it turns and runs the other way.
analogy.breaks: Water really flows in and out of the basin; the emf is a push round the coil, and nothing flows through the coil's face. A real tide is not an exact sine wave, and its timing is set mostly by the moon and sun, not by a steady turn.

practice.text:
The safe way first: it follows from this lesson's rule that a machine with permanent magnets makes a voltage at its terminals whenever its shaft turns, since turning changes the flux through its coils, so treat a turning machine as live.

- Find where the coil faces the field square-on: the flux is at its most there and the emf is zero.
- A quarter turn on, edge-on, the emf is at its peak.
- As the coil passes face-on, each half turn, the emf and the current it drives reverse.
- To predict a change, ask what it does to how fast the flux changes. With the field held steady, speed scales the peak and the frequency together. Turns, field strength and coil area scale the peak alone.

**Rule of thumb:** The emf follows the change in the flux, not the amount.

**Worked example:** A test coil gives 12 V peak at 25 turns a second. At 50 turns a second the flux changes twice as fast, so the peak is 24 V and the frequency 50 Hz, a period of 1 ÷ 50 = 20 ms. Rewound with three times the turns at 50 turns a second, it gives 3 × 24 = 72 V peak, still 20 ms.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting the biggest voltage where the flux is biggest, face-on. There the flux is not changing for an instant, so the emf is zero.
- Thinking the current stops for half of each turn or travels round the circuit. It reverses.
- Thinking the magnet's field alternates. It stays put; the coil's turning makes the change.
- Thinking speed changes only the frequency. In a simple generator with a steady field it raises the peak too.
- Using cos θ for the emf with θ from face-on. Cos θ is the flux; the emf goes with sin θ.

sources.quote: The emf induced is the negative change in the magnetic flux per unit time.

sources.title: 23.5 Electric Generators - College Physics 2e | OpenStax
sources.quote: A generator with a single rectangular coil rotated at constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field produces an emf that varies sinusoidally in time.

sources.title: EMF from rotating coil
sources.quote: The magnitude of the voltage increases with higher rotation frequency, since that leads to a higher rate of change in the flux.

sources.title: maritime electrical installations - notes on design ...
sources.quote: lagging power factor loads tend to demagnetize the field and terminal voltage is maintained only by increasing the d.c. field current. Therefore, a.c. generators are rated in terms of load current and voltage output, or kilovolt-ampere (kVA) output, at a specified frequency and power factor.

checks.label: The emf induced is the negative change in the magnetic flux per unit time: at every speed, number of turns and field the emf is minus how fast the flux through all the turns changes, worked out from the flux itself, and the emf trace drawn on the spinning screen follows it

A single rectangular coil rotated at constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field produces an emf that varies sinusoidally in time: on every screen with the turning coil and its emf, the coil is drawn at its angle and every drawn point of the emf trace is the peak times the sine of the angle at that time, after a right answer too

The magnitude of the voltage increases with higher rotation frequency, since that leads to a higher rate of change in the flux: across the speed slider the peak rises in step with the turns a second, the flux trace's steepest slope rises with it, and the peak printed on the screen follows

60 Hz is the most common frequency adopted for use on board ship: the last puzzle's coil turns 60 times a second instead of 50, its wave repeats every 1 ÷ 60 s, and at the same field its peak is 100 × 60 ÷ 50 = 120 V

At the opening settings the peak is 100 × 0.5 × 0.01 × 2π × 1 = 3.14 V and the period 1 s; at 2 turns a second it is 6.28 V and 0.5 s; with 200 turns it is 6.28 V and still 1 s; and the screens print exactly these

Edge-on (90°) the flux is 0 and the emf at its peak; face-on (0° and 180°) the flux is 1 and −1 and the emf 0; at 270° the emf is at its peak the other way; the spinning screen ends edge-on, its emf pen at the peak and no band

The band is the field passing through the coil: at every angle dragged its height is the coil's height across the field, 72 × the size of the flux share, and the flux pen sits level with the ringed wire
The push marks and the lamp's current keep their direction from face-on to face-on and reverse as the coil passes face-on, every half turn

Every puzzle's numbers are right, and each accepts only its right answer: the flux share is 0 edge-on and 0.5 at 60°; 3 × 12 = 36 V, with 12 ÷ 3 = 4 V the slip; 20 × sin 30° = 10 V, with 20 × cos 30° = 17.3 V the slip; 100 × 60 ÷ 50 = 120 V, with 100 × 50 ÷ 60 = 83.3 V the slip

Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture gives it away: no flux trace when the flux is asked, no emf trace, lamp current or emf value when the emf is asked, and no changed wave or its label until Check

Turns and field scale the peak and leave the period alone: on that screen, at every setting, the peak is turns × field × 0.01 m² × 2π × 1, the period bracket reads 1 s, and the working multiplies out to the peak shown
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: 'One turn draws one whole wave, so the turns a second are the frequency: 50 for UK mains' holds only for two poles; real alternators often have more pole pairs and make several waves a turn, so turn slower (the brief asked for this line).

'Speed scales the peak and the frequency together' is true only with the field held steady; a real generator's regulator adjusts its field to hold its voltage, as the interactive's own Why? says, so the dossier step overstates it.

'turns far more slowly than a real 50 Hz generator' is not true of every machine: many-pole alternators (hydro sets, ship diesel sets) turn far slower than 50 times a second; compare waves a second instead, and say real machines often have several pole pairs.
